column4: The Prophet is commanded to worship God sincerely in dīn. This makes the source's dictionary sense of dīn as obedience concrete as exclusive worship.
The Prophet says he worships God, making his religion sincere for Him alone. It is a direct lived instance of the source's dīn-as-obedience sense.
The ayah says worship belongs to God alone and that dīn belongs to Him enduringly. This directly supports the source's dictionary sense of dīn as obedience and an established religious way.

When believers are called to God and the Messenger for judgment, their answer is that they hear and obey. This gives a concrete instance of the source's dīn-as-obedience sense; the call to judgment is stated in 24:48–50.
God identifies the straight path as His way and says its signs have been detailed. This is a direct repeated formulation of the source's straight-course sense of istiqāma.
Revelation is described as a light by which God guides to a straight path. It makes the source's upright religious direction concrete as revealed guidance.
The worshippers ask God to guide them to the straight path. This is a direct devotional formulation of the upright course named in the source.
God says He commanded the children of Adam not to worship Satan but to worship Him, “this is a straight path.” The verse joins obedience to the source's straight-course image.
Jesus says God is his Lord and theirs, commands worship of Him, and calls this the straight path. This joins the source's dīn-as-obedience sense to a direct formulation of the upright way.
The ayah says whoever holds fast to God has been guided to a straight path. It gives a specific means of remaining on the upright course described in the source.
God says the straight course belongs to Him while some paths deviate. This gives the source's straight religious way a specific contrast between guidance and deviation.
When challenged to become Jews or Christians to be guided, the answer is to follow Abraham's hanīf way. It is a direct repeated formulation of the upright Abrahamic religion named in the source.
The ayah commands people to follow Abraham's way as a hanīf. It directly supplies another Quranic formulation of the source's hanīf, upright religion.

Abraham is described as neither Jew nor Christian but a hanīf who submitted to God, not an associator. This specifies the religious orientation named in the source and distinguishes it from later labels.

The ayah asks who would turn away from Abraham's way except someone who makes a foolish choice, then says God chose him. It supplies a concrete turning away from the hanīf course described in the source.

In a parable, one figure commands justice and is on a straight path. This brings together the source's q-w-m dictionary branches of justice and uprightness, with the scene contrasting that person with a helpless dependent.

Shuayb commands his people to give full measure and not spread corruption on earth after it has been set right. This joins the source's ṣ-l-ḥ versus fasād distinction to just action in a concrete setting.
In its discussion of orphans, the ayah says God knows the corrupter from the reformer. It directly activates the source's dictionary explanation of ṣalāḥ as the opposite of fasād in deeds.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds are said to have their misdeeds removed and their condition set right. This links the source's faith and ṣāliḥ deeds to God's setting the believers right.
Moses says God gave each thing its created form and then guided it. This is a specific parallel to the source's link between creation and the direction appropriate to that creation.

If “asfala sāfilīn” in the source also allows the bodily reading of decline in old age, this ayah gives a specific parallel: God creates people, then some reach the most decrepit age and lose knowledge. That reading is not developed in the section, so the connection is uncertain.

If the source's descent to “asfala sāfilīn” includes bodily decline, this ayah's human arc from weakness to strength and back to weakness is a concrete parallel. The section itself emphasizes religious direction, so this reading remains uncertain.

If the source's “lowest of the low” is read as an ultimate condemned station, this ayah places hypocrites in the lowest depths of the Fire. That interpretation is not developed in the source section, so the connection is uncertain.
The speakers say they used to deny the Day of Judgment. This is a direct denial formulation for the judgment-sense of dīn that can be heard in the source's closing question.
The resurrected say this is the Day of Judgment. It directly activates dīn as reckoning in a scene of resurrection and accountability.
This identifies the Day of Separation and says it is the day people denied, completing 37:20's Day of Judgment. It directly links the source's denial question to its judgment sense.
After naming deniers of the Day of Judgment in 83:11, this ayah specifies that the denier is every transgressing sinner. It links rejection of dīn to a concrete moral condition.
This says that when the revelations are recited to the deniers, they call them tales of earlier people. It adds the deniers' response to the judgment-denial named in 83:11.

The ayah says what people have earned has covered their hearts. In the surrounding passage about denying the Day of Judgment, it makes conduct a cause of spiritual obscuration, complementing the source's faith-and-deeds distinction.
This says the deniers will be screened from their Lord on that day. It gives a consequence completing the judgment passage that begins by naming denial of the Day of Judgment in 83:11.

The denier of dīn is identified in the next ayah as one who repels the orphan. This gives the source's link between religion and righteous action a concrete social example; 107:1 names the denial itself.
The denier of dīn is also one who does not urge feeding the poor. This gives the source's dīn-as-lived-obedience and righteous-deeds themes a concrete social example; 107:1 names the denial itself.

The ayah asks whether a human does not see that God created him from a drop, yet he becomes a clear opponent. It is a specific creation-to-denial parallel to the source's movement from human formation to denial of dīn.

The human who disputes resurrection forgets his own creation and asks who will revive decayed bones. This supplies the challenge that 36:79 answers, paralleling the source's movement from creation to a question of judgment.
The answer is that the One who produced the bones the first time will revive them. It completes 36:78 and directly joins original creation to return, clarifying the accountability behind dīn.
The ayah says God gives life and death and will gather people on the Day of Resurrection, of which there is no doubt. It directly joins creation and human life to the judgment-sense of dīn.
The ayah says whoever does good does so for himself and whoever does evil does so against himself, then all return to God. It connects the source's righteous deeds to an individual reckoning.

God makes believers firm with the firm word in this life and the Hereafter. This is a specific support-and-steadfastness parallel to the source's q-w-m senses of a sustaining foundation and adherence to the straight course.
